Their problem was that this effort remained tied to an equally firm commitment to the Islamic metaphysical framework as a whole. They were unwilling to disturb the basic articles of faith on which that framework rested.
As a result, they often struggled to create a fully consistent connection between their metaphysical commitments and their rational and, at times, realistic approach.
This produced tensions in the inner logic of some of their most important ideas.
But under the conditions in which their movement developed, this was natural and probably unavoidable. We will return to this when we later examine the Muʿtazilite movement as a whole.
C — The Argument for Human Freedom of Choice
Since freedom of human will and action formed the basis of the Muʿtazilite idea of justice, the Muʿtazilites tried to support this freedom with rational arguments.
These arguments grew out of the same rationalist outlook that connected the different parts of their doctrine.
Let us look at the main ways they tried to prove that human beings freely choose their actions.
First — The argument from immediate experience
We call it this because the Muʿtazilites based it on something a person directly experiences within themselves.

“A person feels within himself that his actions follow his motives and restraints. If he wants to move, he moves; if he wants to remain still, he remains still. Whoever denies this denies something obvious and necessary. If the power that arises in the human being were not capable of bringing about what he intended, he would not experience this within himself.”
This argument begins from an ordinary fact of everyday human life.

When a person performs an action, they experience themselves as acting because certain inner and outer reasons lead them to act. When they decide not to do something, they experience themselves as holding back because certain inner and outer reasons lead them not to do it.
In both cases, they experience themselves as choosing.
The Muʿtazilites then draw a second conclusion from this.
A person could not experience themselves in this way unless they actually had the power to perform the action they perform, or to refrain from the action they leave undone.
This basic human awareness of acting or not acting is therefore one sign that human power really exists.
And if that power exists, then human freedom of will exists as well.
When al-Shahrastānī presents this argument, he also refers to a distinction we discussed earlier: the Muʿtazilite distinction between necessary movement and voluntary movement.
Necessary movement is completely governed by an objective law independent of human will and power.
Voluntary movement, by contrast, is connected to human will and human power. It depends on the motives that lead a person toward an act and the restraints that hold them back from it.
The presence of these motives and restraints is what allows the person to choose and then decide either to act or not to act.
Second — The argument from divine commands
This argument is based on rational reflection about the nature of religious obligation.
God addresses human beings through commands such as “Do this” and prohibitions such as “Do not do this.”
According to the Muʿtazilites, reason immediately shows that there are only two possible ways to understand such commands. If one proves impossible, the other must be correct.
The first possibility is that the human being is not capable of doing or avoiding what God commands.
But if that were true, the command itself would be foolish.
It would also be self-contradictory, because God would effectively be saying:
“Do this, you who cannot do it.”
Foolishness and contradiction cannot be attributed to God.
There is another problem with this first possibility.
A command is a request for something to be done. A request only makes sense if the person receiving it is actually capable of carrying it out.
If a person has no freedom to choose and therefore no power to fulfill the command, then the request itself becomes meaningless.
And this too cannot be attributed to God.
God’s commands are accompanied by promise and threat: the promise of reward for obedience and the threat of punishment for disobedience.
But if human beings do not possess the power and freedom to choose between obedience and disobedience, then both promise and threat become meaningless.
Reward and punishment would become meaningless as well.
Again, this cannot be attributed to God.
And there is a fourth problem.
If human beings have no choice, there would be no meaningful difference between God addressing a rational person and God addressing an inanimate object.
There would also be no difference between a command that demands something from a responsible person and a command that merely subjects something to force or demands the impossible.
The second possibility follows from the failure of the first.

If it is impossible to say that human beings cannot carry out God’s commands because they lack freedom, then we must recognize that human beings do possess freedom of choice in the actions God commands or forbids.
We can see that this Muʿtazilite argument from divine commands is essentially the same reasoning that lies at the foundation of their whole idea of justice.
Third — The argument from ordinary social understanding
Like the first argument, this one also begins from real human life.

It begins from the fact that people naturally understand, through ordinary practical reason, that when we give one another commands, prohibitions, praise, blame, or warnings, we assume that the person we are addressing has the freedom to choose.
Al-Shahrastānī presents the Muʿtazilite argument like this:

“Leave religious obligation aside—that is, imagine for a moment that there were no religious law. Is it not normal and familiar among us for people to address one another with commands and prohibitions, to attribute good and evil to someone who chooses freely, to ask them to perform good actions and warn them against bad ones, and then to reward or punish them accordingly?

“Anyone who denies this has stubbornly stepped outside the bounds of reason. There is no point arguing with such a person except in the way one argues with a sophist: insult him and treat him unjustly. If he becomes angry at the insult, feels pain at the injustice, and tries to defend himself or respond, then he has admitted that the person who dealt with him did something. Otherwise, why did he become angry and hurt? And why did he attribute the act to that person?
“If he tries to respond in kind, he has also admitted that the other person committed an act that deserves a corresponding response.”
Beyond the general argument we have already described, this passage tries to force the opponent to accept the principle through his own practical behavior.
Suppose someone is debating the issue and is then harmed by an action that makes him angry or causes him pain.
If he becomes angry or feels hurt, then in practice he has already admitted that the act which caused his anger or pain was freely performed by the person who did it.
And if he then believes that person deserves some response or punishment, he has also admitted that the person was responsible for what he did.
Otherwise, why should he deserve any response at all?

We can now see how deeply the Muʿtazilites were concerned with human freedom of action, with the human capacity to use that freedom, and with the relationship between freedom and moral, social, and religious responsibility.
These questions occupied some of the deepest and widest areas of Muʿtazilite intellectual activity.

Seen in this light, we can also understand how these same concerns drew them toward their distinctive idea of justice—an idea that set them apart from the other Muslims of their time and exposed them to some of the fiercest opposition and hardship.

We can also see how the question of the human being, in all its different aspects, sometimes drew the Muʿtazilites toward starting points rooted in reality, and at times even toward positions that were materialist in the philosophical sense.
Through the force of their own logic and rationalism, the issue pulled them away from a purely metaphysical world and toward the actual natural and social world.

It also brought them close to a scientific way of thinking, despite the abstract and highly conceptual form their thought still took and despite the fact that they lacked the practical tools of experimentation that such thinking would eventually require.
There is nothing surprising about the fact that the question of the human being drew them in this direction.
The question itself had real roots. As we suggested at the beginning of this chapter, its hidden origins lay in actual social conditions.
D — Actions Generated by Human Actions
One striking feature of Muʿtazilite thought is the way its thinkers keep following a single idea or problem as far as it can go.
They constantly open up new sides of every question they examine.
Sometimes they do this in a completely abstract way. At other times their reasoning remains indirectly connected to concrete life.
A good example of the second kind is their discussion of what Muʿtazilite writings call actions generated by human actions.
Once the Muʿtazilites had established that a person is responsible for an act because it comes from that person’s own free will, their method pushed them toward a further question.
What about the actions or effects that normally follow from an act a person performs directly?
Are these later effects also created by the person because they arise from an act the person freely chose?
And if so, is the person responsible for them just as they are responsible for the original act?
At first, this may sound like a purely theoretical question, or even an exercise in abstract reasoning.
But the examples the Muʿtazilites use show that the question has an inner logic closely connected to real life.
Suppose someone strikes another person and the person who is struck feels pain.
There are now two events: the act of striking and the pain that follows.
The first clearly comes from the person who struck the blow. That person is responsible for it because they freely chose to do it.
But what about the second event—the pain produced by the blow?
Should the pain also be attributed to the person who struck, because it was generated by that person’s act?
If so, the person is responsible for the pain as well.
Or should the pain not be considered that person’s act because it was not something they did directly, in which case they would not be responsible for it?
So the real issue is not merely the abstract question of whether the second event was “created” by the person who performed the first act.
The discussion ultimately concerns real responsibility.
And in this case responsibility includes moral and social responsibility just as much as responsibility within a metaphysical framework.
The Muʿtazilite debate over generated actions therefore did not remain purely theoretical. It also had practical, legal, and social implications.
